passage: Sudha's phone buzzed on the desk during study hour. Tanvir had sent, 'Great, just great,' after she'd told him the bus would be late for the fourth time that week. She stared at the flat words. No emoji. Was he angry with her? Frustrated with the bus? Making a joke? Sudha remembered how Tanvir talked when he was cheerful, an actual bounce, and when he was sarcastic, a low flat drawl. In text she could not hear it. Her thumbs hovered. She typed, 'Are you joking or actually upset?' Tanvir replied a minute later, 'ha, both. Bus is late and I'm going to miss cricket.' She sent back a sympathetic face and said she'd wait with him.

qa.q: What did Tanvir send after hearing about the bus?
qa.a: He sent, 'Great, just great,'.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have felt when he sent that message?
qa.a: He was likely frustrated about the late bus and missing cricket, and possibly a little joking too, as he said 'both'. Sudha could not tell from the flat words alone.

qa.q: What made Sudha's question helpful?
qa.a: She asked directly whether he was joking or upset, so she didn't assume contempt or humour from flat text.

qa.q: How might Sudha have felt staring at the flat message?
qa.a: Sudha probably felt unsure and a little anxious, wondering if Tanvir was angry with her, so she asked directly instead of guessing. 🙂

grounding: Sarcasm can signal frustration, humour or contempt, and in text a clarifying question is fair.

passage:
"Great, just great," said Sangeeta, flatly, dropping her bag as the rain came through the ceiling of the practice room.
"Are you joking?" Gopika asked, looking up from the drum.
"Am I laughing?"
"No. So you're annoyed?"
Sangeeta let out a breath. "Yes. We booked this room a month ago and now the rehearsal's off."
"Okay, that's a real problem. I thought maybe you were teasing me for being late."
"No, I was being sarcastic at the roof." Sangeeta almost smiled. "Sorry, I sound like a villain when I'm cross."
"There's the church hall down the street," Gopika said. "Want to ask?"

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta drop her bag?
qa.a: She was annoyed because the rain was coming through the ceiling of the practice room.

qa.q: Why did Gopika ask whether Sangeeta was joking?
qa.a: Gopika could not tell whether the flat 'great, just great' meant humour, frustration or teasing about being late, and did not want to guess wrong. Gopika's worry about being teased shows the doubt.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that helped after Sangeeta explained?
qa.a: Gopika acknowledged the problem and suggested asking at the church hall, turning the annoyance into a next step.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta's tone sound to someone who didn't know her?
qa.a: It could sound like contempt or anger at the person, which is why a check like Gopika's is fair.

grounding: Sarcasm with flat delivery is easily misread, and a clarifying question resolves it.

passage:
Last month my friend Deepak cancelled our cycling plan at the last minute, for the third Saturday in a row. I texted back, "Great, just great. Love that for me."
In my head it was obviously sarcastic. I was annoyed, and a little hurt.
He replied, "Haha glad you're okay with it! Next week for sure 👍"
I stared at the screen. He'd taken it at face value. Or had he? Maybe he was being sarcastic back. I honestly couldn't tell.
The next day, I asked him straight at school: "When I said 'great', did you know I was annoyed?"
He looked surprised. "No! You sounded chill. Were you joking?"
"Not joking. Annoyed."
"Oh. Sorry. I should've called."
I learned that sarcasm in text is like a whisper in a crowd. Sometimes you have to say it plainly.
- Sarita

qa.q: How many Saturdays in a row had Deepak cancelled?
qa.a: For the third Saturday in a row.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when texting "Great, just great"?
qa.a: Sarita felt annoyed and a little hurt about the repeated cancellations, and hid it in sarcasm.

qa.q: What went wrong in the text exchange, and what fixed it?
qa.a: The sarcasm didn't come through in text, so Deepak read it as genuine; asking plainly the next day cleared it up.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen the text?
qa.a: He read it as Sarita being relaxed and fine with it, since the flat, ironic tone didn't come through.

grounding: The account shows sarcastic text carrying annoyance being misread, and a direct question clearing it up.

passage:
Teacher's note - Lalit, Class 10 science, Monday
When I announced a surprise quiz, Rukmini sighed and said in a flat voice, "Oh wonderful. Exactly what I wanted today." A few students laughed.
Our new student, Mika, who joined from Finland last week, turned to her and said, "Oh good, you like quizzes?" He looked puzzled when the laughing grew louder.
Rukmini's expression changed. She could see he wasn't joking.
I wondered for a moment if her tone had contempt in it, for me or the quiz. I decided it was more likely frustration; she'd told me earlier she'd been up late for a family function.
After class I asked her, "Was that a joke, or were you really fed up?" She said, "Both. Sorry, Sir."
She also went to Mika and explained that "wonderful" had meant the opposite. He laughed and said sarcasm at his old school sounded different.

qa.q: Where had Mika joined from?
qa.a: Mika had joined from Finland last week.

qa.q: What was Rukmini feeling when she said "Oh wonderful"?
qa.a: Rukmini was most likely tired and frustrated after being up late, using sarcasm to show it, though Lalit also wondered about contempt.

qa.q: What did Lalit do to check the meaning?
qa.a: He asked Rukmini privately, "Was that a joke, or were you really fed up?" instead of assuming.

qa.q: What was it like for Mika when the class laughed at his reply?
qa.a: He was probably confused and a little embarrassed, not knowing that "wonderful" was meant sarcastically.

grounding: The teacher's note shows sarcasm carrying frustration being misread by a student from another culture, and clarifying questions sorting it out.

passage:
Tuesday
Rehana came from Dubai for Nani's anniversary puja, and when I came downstairs in my new yellow salwar, she looked at me and said, flat as anything, "Wow. Lovely."
That was it. No smile. My stomach sank. Was that sarcasm? It sounded like sarcasm. Everyone in my class says "lovely" like that when they mean "what are you wearing."
I spent the whole puja feeling like a lemon.
At lunch I couldn't take it. I sat next to her and asked, "Were you joking about my salwar? Honestly."
She looked confused. "No! I love it. I'm just jet-lagged. My face isn't working."
She even asked where I got it.
So the flatness was tiredness, not sarcasm. I'd have spent the whole visit hating her if I hadn't asked.
- Rajni

qa.q: Why did Rehana come from Dubai?
qa.a: Rehana came for Nani's anniversary puja.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling during the puja?
qa.a: Rajni felt hurt and self-conscious, "like a lemon," believing Rehana had been sarcastic about the salwar.

qa.q: Which choice of Rajni's worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking plainly whether Rehana was joking worked, because it revealed the flat tone was jet lag, not sarcasm.

qa.q: How might Rehana have felt if Rajni had stayed cold all visit?
qa.a: Rehana would probably have felt confused and rejected, not knowing her tired voice had been misread.

grounding: The diary shows a flat "Wow. Lovely" being mistaken for sarcasm, and a clarifying question revealing it was tiredness.
